analysis.one_liner: Requires disabled people to give businesses 60-120 days notice before suing over entrance barriers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received any vote: introduced with one Republican sponsor and 13 Republican cosponsors, it sat in a House Judiciary subcommittee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Americans with Disabilities Act so that a person who encounters a structural barrier to entering a store or other public place — a missing ramp, an inaccessible doorway — could not sue the owner right away. They would first have to send a written notice identifying the barrier, then wait 60 days for the owner to describe planned fixes, and if a fix is promised, wait another 120 days for the work before going to court. Lawsuits are the main way disabled individuals can enforce these access rules, so the bill would add months of delay before a business could be compelled to act.
analysis.who_benefits: Business and property owners — particularly retail stores, restaurants, and small businesses — facing lawsuits or the threat of them over entrance barriers. They would get 60 to 180 days of advance notice and an opportunity to fix the problem, settle, or draft improvement plans before any litigation, and some barriers might simply never be challenged in court.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Store and property owners facing ADA suits

how_it_helps.text: Owners would receive a written notice specific enough to identify the barrier before any suit could be filed, giving them a chance to fix it without litigation.
Owners would have 60 days to provide a written description of planned improvements, and if they do, an additional 120 days to remove the barrier before a lawsuit could begin.

analysis.who_pays: People with disabilities who encounter barriers to entering public accommodations. They would have to document and mail notices and then wait out 60- to 180-day windows before they could enforce their right of access, and enforcement would fall further on individuals because Justice Department enforcement of accessibility rules is limited.
analysis.who_pays_short: Disabled customers barred from accessible entry

drawbacks.text: The bill would delay or foreclose the primary enforcement tool disabled people have for access rights, since a person could not sue for up to 180 days after notifying an owner of a barrier.

An owner who provides only a written 'description of improvements' — not actual fixes — would still postpone litigation by another 120 days, and nothing in the bill penalizes a plan that is never carried out.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a genuine complaint: businesses, especially small ones, have been hit with lawsuits over entry barriers they were unaware of, and a notice-and-cure period is a fair ask in principle. But the version proposed was lopsided — up to 180 days of delay per barrier, with no penalty for promised fixes that never happen — and the cost falls on disabled customers who rely on private lawsuits precisely because public enforcement is thin. A narrower cure period with a fix deadline would have balanced the two sides better.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 2013, sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then passed to a subcommittee two months later, and no one ever acted on it again before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ken Calvert introduced the bill on March 6, 2013, joined by 13 Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
On April 8, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice, where it stayed.
No committee vote, floor action, or further referral occurred before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Disabled people who use private lawsuits to enforce access to stores and public places kept that tool intact; business owners facing barrier lawsuits gained nothing. The bill's death in committee means the status quo — including the serial-lawsuit practices it aimed to curb — continued unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Disabled people relying on ADA lawsuits

for.name: Rep. Ken Calvert
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require notice and a cure period before ADA barrier lawsuits.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 13 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill and no roll-call vote ever occurred, since it died in committee.

industries.industry: Retail stores, restaurants, and commercial property owners
industries.note: The bill would give these owners 60 to 180 days of notice and an opportunity to promise fixes before anyone could sue over an inaccessible entrance. Its benefit to owners comes directly at the expense of disabled customers' ability to enforce access quickly.

industries.industry: Civil rights and disability-rights plaintiff attorneys
industries.note: A mandatory pre-suit notice and waiting period would reduce the volume of ADA barrier cases and the settlements that flow from them. Those suits are also the main channel through which disabled people get barriers removed, so the attorneys' loss tracks the public's loss here.
